posts.title: 5 Ways People Can Tell AI Wrote Your Post
posts.desc: Five common giveaways that make a post read like a robot wrote it, with a quick fix for each.
body: You wrote the post. Or you asked an AI to write it and hit publish. Either way, people scroll past it and you don't know why. I'll tell you why.

Your reader has seen ten thousand of these. They can smell the machine from across the feed, and they do not forgive it. Most of the time it's the same five habits. Learn them and you'll never publish a limp post again.
"Ever wondered why your posts get no sales?"
Nobody has ever wondered that out loud. Nobody talks like that. Start with the point instead. Say what you saw or what you did.
Fast, simple, effective. Clear, concise, compelling. AI loves a list of three like a cult loves a robe. Real people say one thing and move on. Pick the best word and cut the other two.

"Unlock your potential." Unlock it with what? Whose door? Who has the key? "Elevate your business." Elevate it to where, exactly, the second floor? "Game-changer." Every product is a game-changer. That's how you know none of them are.
These words sound important and say nothing. Swap each one for the thing that actually happens. What does the reader get? What do they do on Monday?
4. A tidy bow at the end
"At the end of the day, success is a journey."
Stop one line early. End on your last real point or a plain question. A post doesn't need a ribbon.
A post with no story, no name and no mess is easy to spot. Add one real detail only you would know. A number from your week. A mistake you made. A customer question.
If you would never say it to a friend, it does not go in the post.
Read it out loud. If it sounds like a press release, change it.
Cut the first sentence. Most posts start better on the second one.
Add one detail from your own life.
That's five. There are more, and each one has a 30-second fix. I put them all in one checklist with before and after rewrites, so you can fix a post in a couple of minutes.

posts.title: The Small Words That Get People to Reply
posts.desc: Simple word swaps that make people more likely to reply, call or buy. No tricks, just clearer writing.
body: When nobody replies to your message, it's rarely the offer. It's the words around it. Small changes are the difference between a message that gets ignored and one that gets an answer.
Say what you mean, with a reason
That gets a maybe, which is a no that's too polite to say so. Try "Can you look at this? I'm stuck on one thing." It gives the person a reason, and a reason makes yes easier.
"Let's hop on a call to discuss" is a big ask. "Want me to send it over?" is a tiny one. People say yes to tiny.

You do not ask a stranger for the whole sale on the first message. You don't propose on the first date. You ask for the next small step. Then the next one. That's the whole trick, and it's embarrassing how well it works.
"Grow your business" is vague. "Get your first sale this month" is something a person can picture. Numbers, names and plain nouns beat adjectives every time.
Write "you", not "people" or "businesses". Picture one reader. Sentences get shorter and warmer without any effort.
Add one reason to every ask. Shrink the ask until it's easy to say yes to.
Replace one vague word with a specific one.
Cut anything you would not say out loud.
I keep a list of the words I use when I want someone to reply, call or buy, with examples of how they sound in real messages. It's free, and it's short enough to use today.

posts.title: Do You Need a Website to Make Your First Sale?
posts.desc: What you actually need online to sell your first thing, and how to get it for free in an afternoon.
body: Short answer: you don't need a big one. You need one page that says what you sell, and a way for people to hand you their email or buy.
One clear headline that says who it's for and what they get.
A short description of the offer in plain words.
One button or one signup box. Not five.
Your name and a way to reach you.
A logo designer. A ten-page menu. A blog. A custom domain on day one. Those are the things that keep people stuck for months, polishing a front door to a house with no furniture.
They're fine later. Later is the word that matters.

Usually it's the blank page. You don't know what to write, so you open ten tabs, compare tools and never publish. The fix is to give an AI assistant one clear set of instructions and let it build the first version, then change what you don't like.
It will never be ready. Ready is a place that does not exist. Ship the ugly version and fix it in public.
Free hosting exists and it works. You can get a one-page site and a signup page live without paying for anything. Add your own domain later when you have a reason to.
One page. One offer. One button. Publish it today.

I wrote one prompt that builds a one-page site and a free signup page with Claude, plus a walkthrough for the free hosting. You paste it in, answer a few questions and publish. It's free, and it's where I'd start.
